story.headline: Worries over AI spending sank Asian shares and pulled US bond yields to one-month lows, nudging the dollar lower. The Bank of Japan held rates but said inflation has reached its goal, and the yen firmed.

reads.policy: Most central banks still lean toward higher rates because of energy-driven inflation. The Bank of Japan held but said inflation has reached its goal, its clearest hint yet of a December hike. The Fed is still expected to hike in December, though falling US yields show markets testing that view.
reads.growth: The US economy is still growing far faster than Europe's and Japan's. A slide in AI-linked shares is the new worry, because a lasting fall could hit spending and investment. Euro-area growth figures this morning show whether Europe is stalling.
reads.inflation: Energy keeps prices high nearly everywhere. Japan's central bank now says underlying inflation is at its goal, and Australian business prices are still climbing. Euro-area and US wage figures today show whether pressure is spreading beyond fuel.
reads.risk: Worries over AI spending sent shares sharply lower in Asia, and money ran to US Treasuries, the yen and the franc. The dollar did not gain, because falling US yields cut its rate edge. Talk of new US strikes on Iran adds a second source of nerves.
reads.tot: Oil rose back near $116 on reports of new US military options against Iran, and is heading for a fourth monthly gain. That keeps helping exporters like Canada and Australia and costing importers like Japan and the euro area.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and the loonie's climb since Canada's rate hike puts those bets under pressure. Their bets against the euro are the largest in years, so good euro news could force them to buy it back. Fresh figures come Friday afternoon.
reads.fiscal: France's budget fight is still unresolved and keeps a weight on the euro, with a vote on taxes due November 3. The European Central Bank says it has tools to calm disorderly bond selling. The UK Budget passed calmly, so British bonds and the pound took it in stride.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28, but two officials voted to hike, and strong US growth figures since then keep a December hike likely. A slide in AI-linked shares has pulled US yields down, which tests how firmly markets believe it.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal, kept up by high energy prices, and the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter.
fed.watch: US wage figures Friday and the October jobs report next week: firm readings would make a December hike close to certain, soft ones or a deeper stock slide would loosen it.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and said more may be needed. That has narrowed the gap with US rates and helped the loonie.
boc.priced: December: another hike possible, about a coin toss.
boc.why: Higher energy prices have lifted Canadian inflation, and the bank raised its inflation forecasts sharply.
boc.watch: Canada's August growth figures at 7:30 AM CT Friday and inflation figures in November, which will shape the odds of a December hike.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% on October 28, but it says more tightening is likely. That makes December a live meeting and limits the kiwi's fall.
rbnz.priced: December: a hike possible; no firm odds yet.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target, and firms say they plan to raise prices more.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand job and price figures before the December 9 decision, and anything Governor Anna Breman says about timing.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% on October 29, and President Christine Lagarde said a hike was discussed, pointing to December. She will step down early, in February, which markets say does not change the policy path.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation well above the 2% goal, even as growth slows and lending tightens.
ecb.watch: Euro-area inflation and growth figures at 5:00 AM CT Friday, and whether worries over French government debt return.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on October 30, but one member voted to hike and the bank said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal. That points to a December hike, which would give the yen some support.
boj.why: The bank now judges inflation to be running at its goal and sees upside risks, with prices rising beyond energy and the jobs market tight.
boj.watch: Governor Kazuo Ueda's comments after the decision, Japanese wage figures, and any move by Tokyo to buy yen; the next decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates on November 3 after inflation ran hotter than it forecast. That supports the Aussie.
rba.why: Underlying inflation is running above the bank's own forecasts, and business-level prices are still climbing.
rba.watch: China's factory surveys Friday night, then the decision at 9:30 PM CT Monday, November 2.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, and the debate is already about December. Cooling UK lending is a sign higher rates are biting.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, driven by energy and fuel, with service prices still sticky.
boe.watch: The decision on November 5 at 6:00 AM CT, and whether the bank hints at a second hike in December.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and has said it is less ready to fight a weaker franc. Swiss inflation is low, so the franc mostly moves on global fear and calm, and it is gaining as shares fall.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Inflation is below target, so the bank has no reason to raise rates while others do.
snb.watch: Swiss inflation figures next week and the global mood; the next decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near the top of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates in December and US inflation runs hot. Falling US yields during a stock scare have taken some of that edge away.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, which keeps US rates high.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, mostly on fuel, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is slowing, energy imports cost more, and France's budget fight weighs on it. The European Central Bank still leans toward a hike in December, which gives it some support.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank held in October and points to a hike in December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area business surveys and economic sentiment keep missing forecasts, with France back in decline.
notes.inflation: Prices are still rising fast in the pipeline, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out.
notes.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: France's unresolved budget and heavy debt keep investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound scores well because the Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates in November, inflation is high and the economy is holding up. It is at its strongest against the euro in about 17 months.

notes.policy: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates on November 5, among the most likely hikes of any major bank.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. The Bank of Japan now says inflation has reached its goal, so a December hike could start to change that.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan held in October and its rate is still far below others', though it now points toward a December hike.
notes.risk: The yen gains when investors look for safety, as it did when shares fell, and Tokyo's warnings limit how weak it gets.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is below target, which keeps the Swiss National Bank from raising rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, and it rose as shares fell.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because the Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates in November and high commodity prices bring money in. A weakening job market is the main drag.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates on November 3, which supports the Aussie.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected, and business prices are still climbing, which keeps hikes coming.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and resources abroad, so high prices bring money into the country.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and high oil prices bring money in. Growth is the soft spot.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and may do so again in December, which narrows the gap with US rates.
notes.growth: Canadian spending has been only modestly firm, which leaves growth the weak spot.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so high crude prices bring money into the country.

NZD.summary: The kiwi fell after New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, but the bank still expects to tighten later. A steady economy and firm export prices limit the damage.

notes.growth: New Zealand's services sector keeps growing, and business confidence rose in October.
notes.risk: The kiwi tends to do well when markets are calm, so a stock scare caps it.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
